title: Life Stress and Facial Expressions of Emotion in Individuals at Clinical High Risk for Psychosis
abstract: Psychosis is a devastating mental illness that is characterized by alterations in emotional functioning. A growing body of work has found links between life stress (e.g., abuse, bullying) and alterations in facial expressions of emotion (e.g., joy) among individuals with psychotic disorder such as schizophrenia. However, to date, there is limited work determining whether life stress is related to alterations in facial expressions of emotion prior to the onset of psychosis, among individuals described as clinical high-risk (CHR). This area of research is needed because potential relationships may inform our understanding of the etiology of psychosis given that many of these individuals are suggested to develop psychosis within a short window of time. As such, the current study sought to determine whether life stress was related to alterations in joy facial expressions of emotion among 75 CHR individuals and 79 age-matched healthy controls. We focused on joy expressions which were deduced from 1-minute video-recorded clinical interviews and measured on a second-by-second basis using the Facial Action Coding System (FACS) coding system. Measures of life stress included traumatic stress (e.g., experienced a life-threatening situation) extracted from the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-IV and interpersonal stress (e.g., bullying) assessed using a parent-report measure. Findings revealed that, overall, CHR individuals showed reduced joy expressions when compared to controls. Additionally, among CHR youth (but not healthy controls) a history of life stress was associated with lower joy facial expressions. These data shed light on our understanding of emotional alterations and psychopathology.
